newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana says U.S. veto leaves top U.N. job open.
newsitem.headline: Ghana says U.S. veto leaves top U.N. job open.

text.p: Ghana said on Wednesday that the U.S. veto of Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali for a second term as U.N. secretary-general opened the door for other African candidates, such as Ghana's Kofi Annan.

But other African nations were more cautious in their initial comments in line with an Organisation of African Unity decision in Cameroon in July to reject U.S. lobbying and throw its weight fully behind Boutros-Ghali.
Foreign Minister Obed Asamoah told Reuters that Ghana was ready to propose Ghanaian Under-Secretary-General Kofi Annan, who heads U.N. peacekeeping operations.

"Ghana, along with other members of the Organisation of African Unity, supported the candidature of Boutros-Ghali but with the U.S. veto the door is open for Ghana and other countries to support another candidate," he said by telephone.
"We are prepared to propose and support Mr Kofi Annan."
U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright voted against a new five-year term for Boutros-Ghali on Tuesday, on grounds that the U.N. needed someone more amenable to reform.
But Boutros-Ghali's supporters, a majority of U.N. members plus 14 of the powerful Security Council's 15 members, appear to have no intention of giving up without a fight.

The Council has agreed to give priority to candidates from Africa on the grounds that if Boutros-Ghali is denied the second term given his predecessors, he should at least be followed by another African.
Diplomats in New York and elsewhere and other U.N. watchers are juggling with a string of names -- some established heavyweights, others less likely candidates at first glance.

They include OAU Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim of Tanzania and Hamid Algabid, secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference, who has been formally proposed by his native Niger.

James Jonah, Sierra Leone's U.N. ambassador and a former U.N. under-secretary-general, is another name mentioned. Jonah successfully organised multi-party national elections in his war-ravaged home country early this year.

One name on some lips is Graca Machel, widow of Mozambique's independence president Samora Machel and close friend of South Africa's Nelson Mandela. She has just concluded a mammoth U.N. report on the Impact of Armed Conflict on Children.
Some African nations have been outspoken.

"The United Nations has not done anything tangible for Africa. It is not a serious organisation. We are not concerned about election of the secretary-general right now," Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni told a news conference on Tuesday.
"Seems that the global and international system is practising a special sort of democracy," Egypt's information minister, Safwat Sherif said, quoting President Hosni Mubarak.
Ghana's neighbour, Ivory Coast, the world's top cocoa producer, as many other African nations has yet to comment officially on the U.S. veto.

Foreign Ministry sources said Ivory Coast would work through the OAU but did not rule out presenting their own candidate if Boutros-Ghali stood down. Foreign Minister Amara Essy has been mentioned as a potential candidate.
"We still stand on BBG's candidature being resubmitted. We don't see anything one could have against him," Kenyan Foreign Ministry spokesman David Kikaya said, but he added:
"If the view is that BBG's candidature is not acceptable, I think we would have to get another consensus from the OAU on another candidate."
